title: Persecuted (Matthew 5:10–12)
hookLine: blessed when you're insulted for doing right
last: MAKE PEACE, NOT JUST KEEP IT.

cards: Sometimes doing right costs you. You speak up for someone and get frozen out of the group. You tell the truth and lose the deal.
You refuse to laugh at the joke and become the next joke. Doing right doesn't always get applause. Sometimes it gets punished.

The last of the Beatitudes is the one nobody puts on a coffee mug. After the empty-handed, the mourners, the meek, the hungry, the merciful, the pure and the peacemakers, Jesus blesses the people who get hurt for it.

teach.h: THE SAME PROMISE AS THE FIRST.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Listen to that ending. It's the same promise as the very first beatitude, the poor in spirit.
The list opens and closes with the same words, like bookends, and everything in between lives inside the kingdom.
And notice: for righteousness' sake. Not for being difficult, or rude, or right in an annoying way. For doing what's right.
Then Jesus speaks straight to the people in front of him, not they any more but ye: blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Then comes the strangest instruction in the sermon: "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you."
The Greek for be exceeding glad, agalliasthe, is more than smiling through it. It's the word for jumping for joy. Why rejoice?

Because you're in good company: the prophets walked this road before you. The book of Acts tells how the apostles, after being beaten, left rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for his name.
Christians have been persecuted in many times and places, from the first centuries to today, and people of many faiths know that suffering too.

In the second century, Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed: the more Christians were killed, the more the church grew. For people in that position, this beatitude is not a nice saying.
It's a promise that their story doesn't end in the cell.

how: Christians remember martyrs on their feast days, and many churches set aside a day or a Sunday each year to pray for Christians who are persecuted around the world.

games.q: you're one of the disciples on the hillside. Jesus says people will insult you and lie about you for his sake. what does he tell you to do?
games.why: "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad." not because pain is good, but because the prophets walked the same road.

practice: Around the world, some Christians face prison, violence or losing their homes for what they believe; picture one of them: a pastor in a cell, a family that had to flee, a teenager mocked at school for praying.
If you pray, you can pray for them now, by name if you know one. If you don't pray, simply hold them in mind, and wish them courage and safety.
